newsitem.title: FINLAND: Copper concentrates seen closely balanced -analyst.
newsitem.headline: Copper concentrates seen closely balanced -analyst.

text.p: Copper concentrate supply and demand will be in a relatively close balance over the next few years before moving into a substantial deficit in the year 2000, analyst Malcolm Southwood of stockbrokers J.B. Were and Son said on Thursday.
"I see no sign of either an acute smelter bottleneck or a severe concentrate shortage during the next three to four years," he told delegates of the Metal Bulletin Base Metal Concentrates conference.
"I think miners, including the big new mines scheduled for development, will be able to sell their concentrate."
An increase in Western concentrate production of an estimated 1.116 million tonnes per year by 2000 will be countered by a rise in Western smelter capacity of 1.517 million tonnes per year.

China's continued role as a major importer of Western concentrate is a key assumption in the forecasts, while large-scale imports into the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) are not expected to resume, Southwood said.
He forecast Chinese imports would ease to 180,000 tonnes of recoverable copper this year, then increase to 270,000 tonnes in 1998, followed by rises of 20,000 tonnes per year in 1999 and 2000.
Meanwhile TC/RCs (treatment charges/refining costs) are expected to remain relatively stable at an average of 25.5 cents/lb (combined) on "standard grade" concentrate at least until 2000.
However, smelters and miners will struggle to come to agreement on charges for an increasing proportion of high grade concentrate expected to emerge from mines such as Escondida, he added.
The average grade in 2000 is forecast at just over 33 percent copper, compared to just over 30 percent in 1994.
The tendency will be for the TC differential between high and standard grade concentrate to widen in terms of dollar to tonne, he said.

"Ideally the smelters would like to establish a formula -- probably increasing the treatment charge by a targeted figure of $1 per tonne for each additional percentage point by which the concentrate exceeds 30 percent copper," he said. --Lida Poletz, London newsroom +44 171 542 2936
